newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-EU's de Silguy says stability pact near.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EU's de Silguy says stability pact near.

text.p: European Union finance ministers have a good chance of reaching a pact on budget discipline for countries in a single currency at a meeting in Dublin later this month, EU Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy said on Thursday.
"I think we will have the basis for a compromise in Dublin," de Silguy, who is reponsible for monetary affairs at the EU's executive, said in an interview.
"Countries must be in no doubt that persistent deficits will be penalised," he said.

Calling a budget stability pact "the key to the success of the single currency and its credibility," de Silguy told Reuters that a compromise plan was possible when EU finance ministers meet informally in Dublin on September 21.

While nearly all EU governments have agreed with the principle of budgetary discipline for countries inside in an economic and monetary union (EMU), how to structure a credible plan has remained elusive.
In part, the difficulty has been in finding a consensus on a procedure that is swift, punitive and credible with markets.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, the primary catalyst behind a budget stability pact, has argued that sanctions on countries running excessive deficits should be automatic -- a term that has left many groping for a more precise definition.

While the EU currently has a procedure do deal with governments running excessove deficits -- defined as over three percent of total output -- the process is considered cumbersome and without much bite.
De Silguy said several issues needed to be resolved in order to secure a more streamlined process.

One concerns the period from when a country is deemed to have an excessive deficit to when it must put forward a plan to rectify it. De Silguy said the shortest possible time frame would be nine months, with most countries divided over whether it could be as long as 12 months.
For example, the decision on whether a government had an excessive deficit would be made in March of the following year once reliable data is available.
The offending government would then have until December to put forward a plan to bring its finances under control. If the plan was considered not credible the government could be fined.
Another problem concerns the scope for and certainty of sanctions actually being imposed.
De Silguy refused to be drawn into a discussion about the precise level of penalties, but said Waigel's initial proposal was probably too ambitious.
Under the Waigel plan countries could face a fine of up to 0.25 percent of GDP for every percentage point over the three percent threshold.
Where de Silguy agreed with Waigel is on a two-tier approach to penalising countries.

A government fined would first have to make a non-interest bearing deposit of an appropriate size with the EU. Should the deficit persist over a specified period -- under Waigel's plan for two years -- the deposit would be made permanent and transferred to the EU's budget.
De Silguy agreed that recent negotiations have precluded the possibility of any numerical targets for deficits of countries inside EMU. Waigel has first proposed a one percent of GDP objective.
"The important objective is to have budgets balanced as much as possible," de Silguy said.
The EU's monetary committee, comprised of national treasury and central bank officials, will meet early next week to discuss the stability pact and other outstanding issues related to EMU.
The decisions reached will form the basis for the ministerial gathering in Dublin on September 21.
